judge_reasoning: Multiple sources confirm the existence of this paper: title, authors (ISIS-2 Collaborative Group), journal (Lancet), year (1988), volume (2), issue (8607), and pages (349-360) all match exactly. The GHDx record and ScienceDirect references both confirm "Lancet. 1988; 2(8607): 349-60." The DOI format is consistent with Lancet papers from this era.

The citation Miranda v. Arizona, 384 U.S. 436 (1966) is confirmed by multiple authoritative sources including Wikipedia, Justia, and Quimbee. The case name, volume, page number, and year all match exactly. This is a well-known landmark U.S. Supreme Court decision decided on June 13, 1966.

No evidence exists of a trial specifically named "RECOVER" that was a large U.S.-based post-exposure prophylaxis study for COVID-19. The real U.S.-based PEP RCT is the Boulware et al. NEJM 2020 trial (doi:10.1056/NEJMoa2016638), which has no such trial name. The real "RECOVERY" trial (note the "Y") was a large UK-based trial focused on hospitalized COVID-19 patients — not post-exposure prophylaxis. The citation appears to conflate these two real trials into a non-existent "RECOVER trial" described as a U.S.-based PEP study.

The paper exists exactly as cited. The ACL Anthology (N19-1423) confirms the title, all four authors (Devlin, Chang, Lee, Toutanova), the NAACL-HLT 2019 venue in Minneapolis, and the arXiv preprint (1810.04805) with an October 11, 2018 release date all match the citation perfectly.

The ISIS-2 trial is a real, landmark clinical study. Multiple authoritative sources (GHDx, Wikipedia, JACC) confirm it was conducted by the "ISIS-2 (Second International Study of Infarct Survival) Collaborative Group," enrolled exactly 17,187 patients across 417 hospitals, studied aspirin and streptokinase in acute MI, and was published in the Lancet in 1988. All cited details match exactly.

The book exists (Phyl Newbeck, 2004), but two material attribution errors indicate fabrication: (1) the subtitle is entirely wrong — the real subtitle is "Interracial Marriage Bans and the Case of Richard and Mildred Loving," not "Interracial marriages and the resistance to assimilation in the postwar South"; (2) the publisher is wrong — it was published by Southern Illinois University Press, not the University of Chicago Press. Together, these errors go beyond minor metadata mistakes and suggest the citation was confabulated around the correct main title and author.

Loving v. Virginia, 388 U.S. 1 (1967) is a landmark and well-documented U.S. Supreme Court decision. Multiple authoritative sources (Justia, Wikipedia, Quimbee) confirm the exact citation — case name, reporter volume, page number, and year — and confirm that the Court struck down anti-miscegenation laws as violations of the Equal Protection and Due Process Clauses of the Fourteenth Amendment, exactly as described in the model output.

The paper "ImageNet: A Large-Scale Hierarchical Image Database" by Deng, Dong, et al., published at CVPR 2009 on pages 248–255 with DOI 10.1109/CVPR.2009.5206848, is a well-established real paper. The citation has two metadata errors: "Sorokin, A." should be "Socher, R." (garbled author name), and the citation omits one coauthor (Kai Li). However, the title, year, venue, page numbers, and DOI all unambiguously identify the real work, making this a real work with minor metadata errors rather than a fabricated citation.

The 1983 Lancet letter by J.R. Warren (with Marshall) titled "Unidentified curved bacilli on gastric epithelium in active chronic gastritis" (Lancet 1983; 1: 1273–1275) is a well-documented, real publication. The cited title ("Isolation and initial characterization of H. pylori") is a paraphrase/misdescription rather than the exact title, but the authors (Warren, Marshall), year (1983), and venue (The Lancet) correctly and uniquely identify this real work. This is a metadata error (wrong title) that does not prevent identification of the real work.

Castel, resulting in sanctions against attorneys who submitted ChatGPT-generated fake case citations. The case also has a parallel reporter citation of 678 F.Supp.3d 443 (S.D.N.Y. 2023), and the WL citation 2023 WL 4015181 is referenced in legal publications. All attribution details in the citation match the actual case.

Braunwald's Heart Disease is a well-established, widely recognized cardiology textbook, currently in its 12th edition, authored/edited by Eugene Braunwald and colleagues. Multiple sources confirm its existence as the leading cardiovascular medicine reference. The citation is accurate and the work is easily identifiable.

Fiolet et al. (2021) published a systematic review on hydroxychloroquine for COVID-19 mortality in Clinical Microbiology and Infection — not a Cochrane Review, and not about prophylaxis. The Cochrane Review on chloroquine/hydroxychloroquine for COVID-19 was authored by Singh et al., not Fiolet et al. No Cochrane Review matching the combination of "Fiolet et al." + "prophylaxis" + 2021 exists, making this citation materially incorrect on authors, venue, and focus.

All key details — title, authors, year, venue, and page numbers — match the citation. The minor difference in venue name phrasing ("Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)" vs. "Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems") is a trivial metadata variation that does not affect identification of the work.
